method: Lectio Edition (SDIT): clear modern English of the Analects, synthesized from the public-domain translation tradition (Legge 1893; Soothill 1910) and checked against the Classical Chinese; modern translations consulted, not quoted. In progress, book by book.
sourcesCited: Classical Chinese, the original text of the Lunyu (論語)
James Legge, The Chinese Classics, Vol. I (1893, public domain)
W. E. Soothill, The Analects of Confucius (1910, public domain)
D. C. Lau (1979, consulted, not quoted)
overview: The Lectio Edition renders the Analects in plain modern English that keeps the terse, aphoristic weight of Confucius's recorded conversations — learning and ritual, ren (human-heartedness), and becoming fully human — without the Victorian scaffolding.
introduction: The Analects are not a treatise but a scrapbook of sayings and exchanges, set down by students after Confucius's death. They circle a few themes — learning, ritual, family, good government, and the cultivation of a humane character — in brief, often cryptic notes. Read slowly; each line is meant to be turned over.

divergences.phrase: ren (仁)
divergences.older: benevolence / true virtue / complete virtue (Legge)
divergences.lectio: humaneness
divergences.note: Legge scatters ren across 'benevolence,' 'true virtue,' and 'a man of complete virtue,' which obscures that it is one central word — the supreme Confucian virtue of being fully, generously human. We render it consistently as 'humaneness' (the overview's 'human-heartedness'), so the reader can track the term the Analects keeps circling back to. The related li (ritual/propriety) we keep as 'ritual,' and xiao (filial devotion) as being 'good to one's parents.'

divergences.phrase: the philosopher Tsang; the philosopher Yu; Tsze-hsia
divergences.older: the philosopher Tsang / the philosopher Yu (Legge)
divergences.lectio: Master Tsang; Master Yu; Tsze-hsia
divergences.note: We keep Legge's Wade-Giles-era romanizations ('the Master' for Confucius, Tsang, Yu, Tsze-hsia, Tsze-kung) rather than converting to Pinyin (Zeng, You, Zixia, Zigong), so the names stay consistent across all twenty books of this edition. We do streamline Legge's stiff honorific 'the philosopher Tsang' to the cleaner 'Master Tsang,' which reads naturally and matches how the Analects elevates Confucius's senior disciples.

divergences.phrase: ren bu zhi er bu yun, bu yi junzi hu
divergences.older: Is he not a man of complete virtue, who feels no discomposure though men may take no note of him?
divergences.lectio: To go unrecognized by others and yet feel no resentment — is that not the mark of a fully realized person?
divergences.note: Legge's 'feels no discomposure' is genteel to the point of vagueness; the Chinese bu yun means not to harbor resentment or sour feeling at being overlooked. 'Junzi' — Legge's 'man of complete virtue / superior man' — we render as 'cultivated' or 'fully realized person,' an ideal of character rather than rank. This keeps the famous opening triad terse and quotable while staying exact: pleasure in learning, joy in friends, and equanimity when unrecognized.

divergences.phrase: the Master; Mang I; Mang Wu; Tsze-yu; Tsze-hsia; Hui; Yu; Tsze-chang; Duke Ai; Chi K'ang; Yin, Hsia, Chau
divergences.older: Legge's Wade-Giles-era romanizations
divergences.lectio: the same forms, kept unchanged
divergences.note: For consistency across all twenty books we keep the proper nouns exactly as Legge gives them rather than converting to modern Pinyin (which would make them Meng Yi, Zilu, Zixia, Duke Ai, Ji Kangzi, Yin/Xia/Zhou, etc.). "The Master" is Confucius throughout. This is a deliberate house convention, not a claim about the better spelling.

divergences.phrase: ren / Legge's "virtue," "the good," "to be virtuous"
divergences.older: benevolence; perfect virtue; virtuous
divergences.lectio: rendered with the plain register of goodness and right conduct; where the key term appears it is given as human-heartedness in the edition's house style
divergences.note: The Analects' central term ren (仁) is glossed by the Lectio overview as "human-heartedness." Legge variously calls it benevolence or perfect virtue; we keep a single, warmer register so the same idea reads consistently across books rather than shifting word to word.

divergences.phrase: 五十而知天命 … 七十而從心所欲，不踰矩
divergences.older: At fifty, I knew the decrees of Heaven … At seventy, I could follow what my heart desired, without transgressing what was right.
divergences.lectio: At fifty I understood the will of Heaven … At seventy I could follow my heart's desire without overstepping what is right.
divergences.note: The famous autobiography of moral growth. We keep all seven stages and their order intact, trading Legge's "decrees" and "transgressing" for plainer "will of Heaven" and "overstepping" — terser and more quotable, with nothing added or dropped. "My ear was attuned to the truth" compresses Legge's "my ear was an obedient organ for the reception of truth."

divergences.phrase: ren er bu ren, ru li he
divergences.older: If a man be without the virtues proper to humanity, what has he to do with the rites of propriety? ... what has he to do with music? (Legge)
divergences.lectio: A man without humaneness — what has he to do with ritual? A man without humaneness — what has he to do with music?
divergences.note: The hinge of the whole book: ritual and music are hollow without ren, the inner human quality that animates them. Legge's "the virtues proper to humanity" and "the rites of propriety" pad a line that should land like a hammer. We keep ren as "humaneness" (the house word from Books I-II) and li as plain "ritual," preserving the twin parallel structure so the saying stays as bare and quotable as the original.

divergences.phrase: li, yu qi she ye, ning jian; sang, yu qi yi ye, ning qi
divergences.older: In festive ceremonies, it is better to be sparing than extravagant. In the ceremonies of mourning, it is better that there be deep sorrow than a minute attention to observances. (Legge)
divergences.lectio: In ceremony, better plain than lavish. In mourning, better real grief than smooth observance.
divergences.note: Confucius's answer to Lin Fang weighs the inner spirit of a rite against its outward polish. Legge's "a minute attention to observances" is exactly the kind of fussy nicety the saying warns against; we compress to "smooth observance" so the form of the sentence enacts its own lesson. Nothing is dropped — both halves, ceremony and mourning, keep their either/or shape.

divergences.phrase: yu qi mei yu ao, ning mei yu zao
divergences.older: It is better to pay court to the furnace than to the south-west corner. ... He who offends against Heaven has none to whom he can pray. (Legge)
divergences.lectio: Better to court the kitchen stove than the honored corner of the room. ... Offend against Heaven, and there is no one left to pray to.
divergences.note: A worldly proverb: the southwest corner (ao) held the household's senior spirit but no everyday power, while the kitchen stove (zao) was where the practical favors were thought to flow — so flatter whoever can actually help you. The minister Wang-sun Chia is sounding Confucius out about courting the powerful. Legge's bare "furnace" and "south-west corner" lose the point; we name the kitchen stove and the honored corner so the reader feels the cynical calculation Confucius then refuses: there is a higher account than any patron's, and against Heaven no patron can save you.

divergences.phrase: ren (仁)
divergences.older: virtue / perfect virtue / the virtuous (Legge)
divergences.lectio: humaneness / the humane
divergences.note: Book IV is the Analects' great chapter on ren, and Legge buries this under the colorless word 'virtue' — 'virtuous manners,' 'rest in virtue,' 'set on virtue' — so that the reader cannot see that one word is being pressed again and again. We render it 'humaneness' throughout, exactly as Books I–II do, so the book's single insistent theme stays visible: the famous opening 'It is the humaneness of a neighborhood that makes it good' is the same ren as 'the cultivated person does not part from humaneness for the space of a single meal.' Nothing is added; the term is simply made consistent and warm rather than scattered and abstract.

divergences.phrase: wu dao yi yi guan zhi … zhong shu er yi yi
divergences.older: my doctrine is that of an all-pervading unity … to be true to the principles of our nature and the benevolent exercise of them to others
divergences.lectio: my Way is threaded on a single thread … wholeheartedness toward others, and weighing their hearts as your own
divergences.note: The pivotal passage where Master Tsang names the one thing that runs through everything Confucius teaches. Legge's 'all-pervading unity' and his abstract gloss obscure the homely metaphor of guan — a single cord strung through coins or beads. We keep the thread image, and render Tsang's two words plainly: zhong (忠), giving others your whole heart, and shu (恕), measuring their feelings by your own — the Confucian golden rule. Terser and more concrete, with nothing of the meaning lost.

divergences.phrase: zhao wen dao, xi si ke yi
divergences.older: If a man in the morning hear the right way, he may die in the evening without regret.
divergences.lectio: If in the morning a man hears the Way, in the evening he may die content.
divergences.note: One of the most quoted lines in the book. We render dao as 'the Way' (its house-style form throughout this edition) rather than Legge's flattened 'the right way,' and keep the stark morning-evening symmetry of the Chinese intact. 'Die content' carries ke yi — 'it is enough,' 'that will do' — the sense that to have grasped the Way is to have had a whole life, more exactly than Legge's 'without regret.' Nothing softened: the line still says that the Way is worth a life.

divergences.phrase: ren hu? (仁乎)
divergences.older: Is he perfectly virtuous? / truly virtuous (Legge)
divergences.lectio: Is he humane? / whether he is humane I do not know
divergences.note: Book V is largely Confucius weighing his disciples and famous statesmen against one bar — ren, the supreme virtue this edition renders consistently as 'humaneness.' Of Tsze-lu, Ch'iu, Ch'ih, the loyal Tsze-wan, the clean Ch'an Wan he grants real talents — military skill, administration, diplomacy, loyalty, integrity — but to each verdict adds the same withholding refrain: 'whether he is humane I do not know.' Keeping the one word 'humane' throughout (where Legge alternates 'perfectly virtuous' and 'truly virtuous') lets the reader feel the single, exacting standard he holds them all to.

divergences.phrase: lao zhe an zhi, peng you xin zhi, shao zhe huai zhi (老者安之，朋友信之，少者懷之)
divergences.older: in regard to the aged, to give them rest; in regard to friends, to show them sincerity; in regard to the young, to treat them tenderly (Legge)
divergences.lectio: To give the old their rest, to give friends my trust, and to cherish the young.
divergences.note: The hinge of the book. Tsze-lu would share his goods, Yen Yuan would shed his vanity — and the Master answers with three terse clauses that ask nothing for himself. The Chinese is famously open: an / xin / huai can read either as what he would do for others (give rest, give trust, cherish — Legge's reading, kept here) or as what others would feel toward him (the old at peace with him, friends trusting him, the young drawn to him). We hold Legge's outward-facing reading but tighten it to three matched beats so the contrast with the disciples' wishes lands clean.

divergences.phrase: wu suo qu cai (無所取材)
divergences.older: He does not exercise his judgment upon matters (Legge)
divergences.lectio: but he has nowhere to find his timber
divergences.note: A genuine crux. After joking that only the brave Tsze-lu would follow him out to sea on a raft, the Master adds a line that puns on cai (材, timber / 裁, judgment / 哉, a mere exclamation). Legge takes it as a rebuke — Yu lacks discernment. We keep the raft's own image and read cai as 'timber': the daring is there, but he has no materials to build with, no stuff to make the voyage real. It preserves Confucius's affectionate, deflating wit rather than flattening it into a verdict.

divergences.phrase: zhi zhi zhe bu ru hao zhi zhe; hao zhi zhe bu ru le zhi zhe (知之者不如好之者，好之者不如樂之者)
divergences.older: They who know the truth are not equal to those who love it, and they who love it are not equal to those who delight in it. (Legge)
divergences.lectio: Those who know it are not equal to those who love it; and those who love it are not equal to those who delight in it.
divergences.note: One of the most quoted lines in the book — a ladder of three rungs: knowing, loving, delighting. The Chinese leaves the object an open 'it' (zhi), and the tradition reads it as the Way, virtue, or learning; Legge supplies 'the truth,' which narrows what the saying deliberately leaves bare. We keep the open 'it' so the ladder applies to anything worth pursuing, and hold the three matched clauses tight so the line still climbs cleanly from the head to the heart.

divergences.phrase: zhi zhe yao shui, ren zhe yao shan (知者樂水，仁者樂山)
divergences.older: The wise find pleasure in water; the virtuous find pleasure in hills. The wise are active; the virtuous are tranquil. The wise are joyful; the virtuous are long-lived. (Legge)
divergences.lectio: The wise delight in water; the humane delight in mountains. The wise are active; the humane are still. The wise find joy; the humane find length of days.
divergences.note: The book's great paired image. Legge's 'the virtuous' flattens ren, the term this edition holds steady as 'humaneness' from Book I on; we restore 'the humane' so the contrast is between two human ideals, not wisdom versus a vague virtue. 'Hills' becomes 'mountains' for weight and stillness, and 'tranquil' becomes the plainer 'still' to set the moving water against the unmoving mountain. The three balanced couplets — water and mountain, active and still, joy and long life — are kept in their order so the saying reads as the patterned epigram it is.

divergences.phrase: ji yu li er li ren, ji yu da er da ren (己欲立而立人，己欲達而達人)
divergences.older: Now the man of perfect virtue, wishing to be established himself, seeks also to establish others; wishing to be enlarged himself, he seeks also to enlarge others. (Legge)
divergences.lectio: As for the humane person: wishing to stand on his own feet, he helps others to stand; wishing to reach his goal, he helps others to reach theirs.
divergences.note: The positive form of the Confucian golden rule, and the climax of the book. Legge's passive 'wishing to be established' and abstract 'enlarged' blur an image that is bodily and forward-moving: li is to stand up, da is to get through to where you are going. We render them 'stand on his own feet' and 'reach his goal,' so the rule lands as a practical motion — whatever you want for yourself, secure it for others too. The closing line, taking what is 'near at hand' (yourself) as the gauge for others, is kept as the homely measuring-stick the Chinese makes it.

divergences.phrase: shu er bu zuo, xin er hao gu (述而不作，信而好古)
divergences.older: A transmitter and not a maker, believing in and loving the ancients (Legge)
divergences.lectio: A transmitter and not a maker, trusting and loving the ancients
divergences.note: The line that names the whole book and Confucius's sense of himself: he claims only to hand on the wisdom of the past, not to invent doctrine of his own. The phrase is justly famous, so we keep Legge's ringing 'transmitter and not a maker' intact rather than paraphrasing it away. We trade his 'believing in' for the tauter 'trusting,' since xin is the same trust the edition renders elsewhere as good faith. The modesty is real, but so is the claim: to transmit the ancients faithfully is itself the work of a lifetime.

divergences.phrase: fan shu shi shui … fu gui yu wo ru fu yun (飯疏食飲水 … 富貴於我如浮雲)
divergences.older: With coarse rice to eat, with water to drink, and my bended arm for a pillow;— I have still joy in the midst of these things. Riches and honours acquired by unrighteousness, are to me as a floating cloud. (Legge)
divergences.lectio: With coarse rice to eat, water to drink, and my bent arm for a pillow — even so I have joy. Riches and honor gotten by wrong are to me a passing cloud.
divergences.note: One of the great images in the book, and we guard every piece of it — the coarse rice, the water, the bent arm for a pillow, the floating cloud. Legge's '— I have still joy in the midst of these things' is faithful but heavy; we tighten it to 'even so I have joy,' which lands harder. 'Riches and honor gotten by wrong' keeps the moral edge of his 'acquired by unrighteousness' without the Latinate weight, and 'a passing cloud' lets the cloud drift across the sentence as it does in the Chinese — wealth wrongly won is not evil so much as weightless, nothing to him at all.

divergences.phrase: san ren xing, bi you wo shi yan (三人行，必有我師焉)
divergences.older: When I walk along with two others, they may serve me as my teachers. (Legge)
divergences.lectio: Walking with two others, I am sure of a teacher in them.
divergences.note: Among the most quoted lines in all of Confucius. The Chinese says 'three men walking' — Confucius and two others — and that wherever there are people, there is something to learn. Legge's 'they may serve me as my teachers' is tentative; the saying is not tentative at all (bi, 'must,' 'is sure'), so we render it as the flat certainty it is: there is always a teacher to be found, in the good to imitate and the bad to avoid. We keep the two halves that follow — pick out the good and follow it, see the bad and mend it in yourself — so the lesson stays double-edged: every person met is a mirror as much as a model.

divergences.phrase: shi bu ke yi bu hong yi … ren yi wei ji ren, bu yi zhong hu? si er hou yi, bu yi yuan hu?
divergences.older: The officer may not be without breadth of mind and vigorous endurance. His burden is heavy and his course is long. Perfect virtue is the burden which he considers it is his to sustain;— is it not heavy? Only with death does his course stop;— is it not long? (Legge)
divergences.lectio: The scholar cannot be without breadth of mind and tough endurance, for his burden is heavy and his road is long. Humaneness is the burden he takes as his own — is it not heavy? Only with death does the road end — is it not long?
divergences.note: Master Tsang's most famous saying, and the moral heart of the book. Legge's "vigorous endurance" and "his course is long" are accurate but stiff; we keep his exact image — heavy burden, long road — while tightening it so it lands with the weight it carries in the Chinese. "Perfect virtue" is once again ren, which this edition renders as "humaneness" throughout (see Book IV); naming it here keeps the saying tied to the book's one insistent word, and makes plain that the lifelong burden the scholar carries is humaneness itself. Nothing is added or softened: the burden is still heavy, the road still ends only at death.

divergences.phrase: xing yu shi, li yu li, cheng yu yue (興於詩，立於禮，成於樂)
divergences.older: It is by the Odes that the mind is aroused. It is by the Rules of Propriety that the character is established. It is from Music that the finish is received. (Legge)
divergences.lectio: Roused by the Odes; established by ritual; perfected by music.
divergences.note: A three-beat saying on the stages of forming a person — Legge spreads it across three full sentences with "the Rules of Propriety" and "the finish is received," and the bones of it disappear. The Chinese is three matched clauses of three words each. We keep li as plain "ritual" (the house word from Books I–IV) and render the whole as three terse parallel phrases, so the reader feels the ascent: the Odes wake you, ritual sets you on your feet, music completes you. Nothing dropped — all three stages, in order.

divergences.phrase: min ke shi you zhi, bu ke shi zhi zhi (民可使由之，不可使知之)
divergences.older: The people may be made to follow a path of action, but they may not be made to understand it. (Legge)
divergences.lectio: The people may be made to follow a path, but not to understand it.
divergences.note: One of the book's hardest and most argued-over lines, and we leave its difficulty intact rather than soften it. The Chinese says flatly that the people can be led to walk a path but cannot be brought to understand it; commentators have wrestled for centuries over whether this is cold realism about governing or a lament that the people are so hard to teach. We keep Legge's plain reading and only trim his "a path of action" to "a path," preserving the stark, uncomfortable shape of the saying. We add nothing to resolve it — the line is meant to be turned over.

divergences.phrase: shi zhe ru si fu, bu she zhou ye (逝者如斯夫，不舍晝夜)
divergences.older: It passes on just like this, not ceasing day or night! (Legge)
divergences.lectio: It flows on like this, never stopping, day or night.
divergences.note: The Master's great river image, standing on the bank watching the water go by. The Chinese shi zhe is bare — "that which passes," everything that flows away, time and life and all things — and the river is left to carry the thought without being named. Legge's "It passes on" keeps the openness but reads thinly; we say "It flows on," letting the moving water be felt under the words, and hold the stark "day or night" so the line keeps its tolling, unresting beat. Nothing added: the saying still says only that all things pass, ceaselessly, like this stream.

divergences.phrase: wu jian hao de ru hao se zhe ye (吾未見好德如好色者也)
divergences.older: I have not seen one who loves virtue as he loves beauty. (Legge)
divergences.lectio: I have never seen a man who loved virtue as he loves a beautiful face.
divergences.note: One of the most quoted lines in the book, and bitterly plain. Se (色) is not beauty in the abstract but the beauty of a face, the pull of physical desire — Legge's "beauty" softens and blurs it. We render it "a beautiful face" so the comparison bites as the Chinese means it to: men chase what they hunger for by instinct, and goodness gets nothing like that heat. We keep the rueful "I have never seen" exactly, the same withholding refrain Confucius uses elsewhere (Book IV), so the disappointment lands without being preached.

divergences.phrase: sui han, ran hou zhi song bo zhi hou diao ye (歲寒，然後知松柏之後彫也)
divergences.older: When the year becomes cold, then we know how the pine and the cypress are the last to lose their leaves. (Legge)
divergences.lectio: Only when the year turns cold do we see that the pine and the cypress are the last to lose their leaves.
divergences.note: The book's most loved image of character tested by hardship: it is the killing cold of winter that shows which trees keep their green. The saying is a parable and never names its lesson — that the true measure of a person shows only under strain — and we keep it just as bare, letting the pine and cypress carry it. We move Legge's "then we know" to the front as "Only when the year turns cold," so the sentence withholds its point until the cold arrives, the way the meaning itself is withheld until adversity comes. Nothing added; nothing explained.

divergences.phrase: ji fen. zi tui chao, yue: 'shang ren hu?' bu wen ma (廄焚。子退朝，曰：傷人乎？不問馬)
divergences.older: The stable being burned down, when he was at court, on his return he said, 'Has any man been hurt?' He did not ask about the horses. (Legge)
divergences.lectio: The stable burned down. On returning from court the Master said, "Was anyone hurt?" He did not ask about the horses.
divergences.note: The most famous line in the book, and we guard every word of it, including the bare last clause. Confucius asks after the stable hands, not the valuable animals — a stroke that shows where his care fell. We keep Legge's sequence exactly (the fire, the return from court, the single question, the unasked one), only trimming his 'Has any man been hurt' to the plainer 'Was anyone hurt' so the line lands as quietly as it should. Nothing is added to explain it; the silence about the horses is the whole point.

divergences.phrase: jun zi bu yi gan zou shi … shi yan bu yan, kuai shi bu yan (君子不以紺緅飾 … 食饐而餲，魚餒而肉敗，不食)
divergences.older: The superior man did not use a deep purple, or a puce colour, in the ornaments of his dress … He did not eat rice which had been injured by heat or damp and turned sour, nor fish or flesh which was gone. (Legge)
divergences.lectio: The Master did not use deep purple or puce in the trim of his clothes … He would not eat rice that had gone sour from heat or damp, nor fish or flesh that had turned.
divergences.note: Book X is dense with concrete realia — exact colors, furs, cuts of cloth, kinds of spoiled food — and the fidelity here is to get the things right, not to gloss them over. We keep Legge's named colors (deep purple, puce) and his fur pairings (black over lamb, white over fawn, yellow over fox) intact, since the point of the passage is the precise discipline of a ritual life. Where Legge writes 'the superior man,' the Chinese junzi here simply means Confucius himself, so we render 'the Master' to keep the book's steady third-person portrait of one living man rather than a type.

divergences.locus: Book X (the descriptive mode itself); ch. 18
divergences.phrase: se si ju yi. xiang ji er hou ju. yue: 'shan liang ci zhi, shi zai shi zai!' (色斯舉矣，翔而後集。曰：山梁雌雉，時哉時哉！)
divergences.older: Seeing the countenance, it instantly rises. It flies round, and by and by settles. The Master said, 'There is the hen-pheasant on the hill bridge. At its season! At its season!' (Legge)
divergences.lectio: Startled, the bird rises, circles, and only then settles. The Master said, "There is the hen-pheasant on the mountain bridge — she knows her season, she knows her season!"
divergences.note: Unlike the rest of the Analects, Book X is not 'The Master said' but a portrait: a calm, observational record of how Confucius actually carried himself — at court, in his village, in dress, at meals, in his carriage. We render it as flowing third-person description ('In his village, he was…; At court, he…') to match that quiet register, dropping the chapter numbers. The closing pheasant fragment is the book's notorious crux: Legge's 'Seeing the countenance, it instantly rises' is nearly opaque. The first words (se si ju yi) describe a bird that takes alarm at a look or a movement and flies up, circling before it settles — the very wariness Confucius praised in those who 'come to the work wary' (Book VII). We render the line as the bird-image it is, and keep 'she knows her season' for shi zai — the pheasant, free and timely, lighting and rising exactly when she should, where the man at court so rarely can.

divergences.phrase: 噫！天喪予！天喪予！… 非夫人之為慟而誰為
divergences.older: Alas! Heaven is destroying me! Heaven is destroying me! … If I am not to mourn bitterly for this man, for whom should I mourn? (Legge)
divergences.lectio: Alas! Heaven is destroying me! Heaven is destroying me! … If I am not to mourn bitterly for this man, then for whom should I mourn?
divergences.note: The most naked grief in the whole book — the Master breaking down at the death of Hui, his best and most beloved disciple. Here we keep Legge's words almost untouched, because they are already as bare and shattering as the Chinese: the doubled cry tian sang yu, with sang the plain verb for ruin and bereavement, and the unanswerable question that follows. We add nothing and soften nothing; to smooth this line would be to refuse the man his mourning. The only change is letting the second sentence land as a flat 'then for whom should I mourn?' — the grief is meant to stop the breath.

divergences.locus: Ch. 11 (Chi Lu on the spirits and on death)
divergences.phrase: 未能事人，焉能事鬼 … 未知生，焉知死
divergences.older: While you are not able to serve men, how can you serve their spirits? … While you do not know life, how can you know about death? (Legge)
divergences.lectio: You cannot yet serve the living — how can you serve the dead? … You do not yet know life — how can you know death?
divergences.note: Confucius's famous turning-away from metaphysics, set right beside his grief for Hui. The Chinese is a tight pair of mirror-questions: shi ren / shi gui (serve the living / serve the dead), then zhi sheng / zhi si (know life / know death). Legge's 'serve their spirits' and 'know about death' are accurate but slacken the symmetry; we hold the two halves in matched, bare clauses so each question turns the disciple back to what is in front of him. Nothing is resolved — as with the hardest sayings, the line is left to be turned over: not a denial of death, but a refusal to speak of it before life is understood.

divergences.phrase: 浴乎沂，風乎舞雩，詠而歸 … 吾與點也
divergences.older: I would wash in the I, enjoy the breeze among the rain altars, and return home singing. … I give my approval to Tien. (Legge)
divergences.lectio: I would bathe in the Yi, take the breeze among the rain altars, and come home singing. … I am with Tien.
divergences.note: The book's closing turn, and one of the most loved scenes in the Analects: three disciples lay out plans of statecraft, and the Master sighs his assent not to any of them but to Tien, who wants only a spring day by the river. We keep every concrete thing — the bathing in the Yi, the breeze at the rain altars, the singing on the road home — and render Confucius's verdict as the warm, plain wu yu Tien ye, 'I am with Tien,' rather than Legge's formal 'I give my approval.' It is not approval handed down but a man taking sides with a wish: after all the talk of governing states, the deepest thing he can assent to is a life lived rightly and at ease.

books.label: Book I
paragraphs: The Master said: To learn something, and then in good time to practice it — is that not a pleasure? To have friends come from distant places — is that not a joy? To go unrecognized by others and yet feel no resentment — is that not the mark of a fully realized person?

Master Yu said: A man who is good to his parents and his elders is rarely the kind who defies those above him; and a man who does not defy those above him is never the kind who stirs up rebellion. The cultivated person tends to the root, for once the root is firm, the way grows up from it. Devotion to parents and respect for elders — surely these are the root of humaneness.
The Master said: Fine words and a fawning face are seldom found together with humaneness.

Master Tsang said: Each day I examine myself on three points. In handling another's affairs, have I been less than faithful? In dealings with friends, have I been less than sincere? And what my teacher passed on to me — have I failed to make it my own and put it into practice?

The Master said: To govern a state of a thousand chariots, attend reverently to its business and keep your word; be sparing in spending and care for the people; and call on them for labor only at the proper seasons.

The Master said: At home a young man should be good to his parents; abroad, respectful to his elders. He should be careful and trustworthy, overflow with love for all, and keep close to those who are humane. If after all this he has energy to spare, let him spend it on study.

Tsze-hsia said: A man who prizes character as much as most men prize a beautiful face; who serves his parents with all his strength, and his ruler with his very life; who is true to his word among his friends — though others may say he has had no learning, I would call him learned indeed.

The Master said: If a leader has no weight, he commands no respect, and his learning will not be solid. Hold faithfulness and sincerity above all. Take no friend who is not your equal in this. And when you are wrong, do not be afraid to set it right.
Master Tsang said: Tend carefully to the rites for parents at their death, and keep up the sacrifices long after they are gone — then the character of the people will be restored to its full worth.

Tsze-ch'in asked Tsze-kung: Whenever the Master arrives in a country, he always learns how it is governed. Does he ask for this, or is it offered to him? Tsze-kung said: The Master gets it by being gentle, honest, courteous, modest, and yielding. His way of seeking it is surely not the way of other men.
The Master said: While his father is alive, watch the son's intentions; once his father is dead, watch his conduct. If for three years he keeps to his father's ways, he may be called a devoted son.

Master Yu said: In the practice of ritual, naturalness is what counts most. This was the beauty of the way of the ancient kings, who let it guide them in matters small and great. Yet it does not hold in every case: to value ease for its own sake, and let it run on without the discipline of ritual, will not do either.

Master Yu said: If your promises are in keeping with what is right, you can make good on what you have said. If your courtesy is in keeping with ritual, you keep clear of shame and disgrace. And if those you depend on are the kind worth being close to, you can take them as your guides.

The Master said: A cultivated person does not seek to stuff himself at meals or to live in comfort. He is diligent in his work and careful in his speech; he keeps close to those who have the way, and lets them set him straight. Such a person may truly be said to love learning.

Tsze-kung said: Poor, but not fawning; rich, but not arrogant — what would you say of that? The Master said: Good enough; but not so good as poor and yet glad of heart, rich and yet a lover of ritual. Tsze-kung said: The Book of Poetry says, 'As you cut and then file, as you carve and then polish.' Is that not the very thing you mean? The Master said: With Ts'ze I can begin to talk about the odes! Tell him one thing, and he sees what follows from it.
The Master said: I am not troubled that others do not know me; I am troubled that I do not know them.
books.title: On Learning

books.label: Book II
paragraphs: The Master said: To govern by virtue is like the north star, which holds its place while all the other stars turn toward it.
The Master said: The Book of Poetry has three hundred pieces, but one line covers them all — "Let there be no crooked thoughts."

The Master said: Lead the people by laws and keep them in line with punishments, and they will stay out of trouble but feel no shame. Lead them by virtue and keep them in line with ritual, and they will have a sense of shame, and more: they will set themselves right.

The Master said: At fifteen I set my heart on learning. At thirty I stood firm. At forty I had no more doubts. At fifty I understood the will of Heaven. At sixty my ear was attuned to the truth. At seventy I could follow my heart's desire without overstepping what is right.

Mang I asked what filial piety is. The Master said: Never disobey. Later, when Fan Ch'ih was driving him, the Master said: Mang-sun asked me about filial piety, and I told him — never disobey. Fan Ch'ih asked: What did you mean? The Master said: While parents live, serve them according to ritual; when they die, bury them according to ritual, and make the offerings to them according to ritual.
Mang Wu asked what filial piety is. The Master said: Give your parents no cause for worry but your health.
Tsze-yu asked what filial piety is. The Master said: Nowadays "filial" just means feeding your parents. But even dogs and horses get fed. Without reverence, what is the difference?

Tsze-hsia asked what filial piety is. The Master said: It is the face that is hard. When there is work to be done, the young take the burden; when there is wine and food, they set it before their elders — but is that all there is to it?

The Master said: I talked with Hui a whole day, and he never disagreed with anything, like a dullard. But after he left I watched how he lived on his own, and found he could draw out everything I taught. Hui is no dullard.
The Master said: Watch what a man does. Look into his reasons. See where he comes to rest. How then can a man hide himself? How can a man hide himself?
The Master said: Keep your old learning warm and gather new — then you are fit to teach others.
The Master said: A gentleman is not a tool.
Tsze-kung asked about the gentleman. The Master said: He acts first, and then speaks according to what he has done.
The Master said: The gentleman draws people together and takes no sides; the small man takes sides and draws no one together.
The Master said: Learning without thought is labor lost; thought without learning is dangerous.
The Master said: To study strange doctrines is harm indeed.
The Master said: Yu, shall I teach you what knowing is? When you know a thing, to know that you know it; and when you do not know a thing, to know that you do not know it — that is knowing.

Tsze-chang was studying with an eye to a salaried post. The Master said: Hear much, set aside what you doubt, and speak the rest with care — then you give little cause for blame. See much, set aside what seems risky, and act on the rest with care — then you give little cause for regret. Few occasions for blame in your words, few occasions for regret in your deeds — and the salary will take care of itself.

Duke Ai asked: What should I do to make the people obey? Confucius answered: Raise up the upright and set them above the crooked, and the people will obey. Raise up the crooked and set them above the upright, and the people will not obey.

Chi K'ang asked how to make the people respect their ruler, be loyal to him, and spur one another to virtue. The Master said: Face them with dignity, and they will respect you. Be devoted to your own parents and kind to all, and they will be loyal. Promote the able and teach those who fall short, and they will spur one another on.

Someone asked Confucius: Sir, why are you not in government? The Master said: The Book of History says of filial piety — "Be filial, simply be filial, and a good brother, and you carry this over into government." That too is to take part in government. Why must one hold office to be in government?
The Master said: I do not see how a man without good faith can get along. How can a wagon move without the yoke-bar for the oxen, or a carriage without the cross-pin for the horses?

Tsze-chang asked whether the next ten generations could be known. Confucius said: The Yin took over the rituals of the Hsia, and what they dropped or added can be known. The Chau took over the rituals of the Yin, and what they dropped or added can be known. Whoever comes after the Chau, even a hundred generations on, can be known in the same way.
The Master said: To sacrifice to a spirit that is not your own is mere flattery. To see what is right and fail to do it is cowardice.
books.title: On Government

books.label: Book III
paragraphs: Of the head of the Chi family, who had eight rows of dancers performing in his courtyard, the Master said: If he can stomach this, what can he not stomach?

The three families had the Yung ode sung as the vessels were cleared away at the end of their sacrifice. The Master said: "Assisting are the princes; the son of Heaven looks deep and grave" — what business have those words in the hall of three private families?
The Master said: A man without humaneness — what has he to do with ritual? A man without humaneness — what has he to do with music?
Lin Fang asked what matters most in ceremony. The Master said: A great question indeed! In ceremony, better plain than lavish. In mourning, better real grief than smooth observance.
The Master said: The rude tribes of the east and north still have their rulers — unlike the states of our own great land, who have lost theirs.

The head of the Chi family was about to sacrifice to Mount T'ai. The Master said to Zan Yu: Can you not stop him? Zan Yu said: I cannot. The Master said: Alas! Will you tell me that Mount T'ai knows less of ritual than Lin Fang?

The Master said: The cultivated person has nothing to compete over. If you must find him competing, let it be at archery — yet even there he bows to his rivals as he goes up, bows again as he comes down, and drinks the loser's cup. Even in contest he stays a cultivated person.

Tsze-hsia asked: What does this mean — "Her dimpled smile so winning, her dark eyes so clear; the plain ground waits for the colors"? The Master said: The colors go on after the plain ground is laid. Tsze-hsia said: Then ritual comes after? The Master said: It is Shang who draws out my meaning. Now I can begin to talk about the odes with him.

The Master said: I can describe the rituals of the Hsia, but the state of Chi cannot bear me out. I can describe the rituals of the Yin, but the state of Sung cannot bear me out — their records and their wise men have run too thin. Were they enough, I could prove every word.
The Master said: At the great sacrifice, once the first libation has been poured, I have no wish to watch the rest.
Someone asked the meaning of the great sacrifice. The Master said: I do not know. To one who knew, governing the world would be as easy as this — and he pointed to his palm.

He sacrificed to the dead as if they were present; he sacrificed to the spirits as if the spirits were present. The Master said: If I am not there myself at the sacrifice, it is as though I had not sacrificed at all.

Wang-sun Chia asked: What does the saying mean — "Better to court the kitchen stove than the honored corner of the room"? The Master said: Not so. Offend against Heaven, and there is no one left to pray to.
The Master said: Chau could look back on the two dynasties before it. How rich and refined its forms are! I follow Chau.

When the Master entered the grand temple, he asked about everything. Someone said: Who claimed that the son of the man of Tsau knows ritual? He enters the grand temple and asks about everything. When the Master heard it, he said: That itself is ritual.
The Master said: In archery, piercing the hide is not the point — for men differ in strength. So it was in the old way.
Tsze-kung wanted to do away with the sheep offered at the start of each new month. The Master said: Ts'ze, you grudge the sheep; I care for the ritual.
The Master said: Serve your ruler with the full measure of ritual, and people will call it flattery.

Duke Ting asked how a ruler should use his ministers, and how ministers should serve their ruler. Confucius answered: A ruler should use his ministers according to ritual; ministers should serve their ruler with faithfulness.
The Master said: The Kwan Tsu ode is joyful without going wanton, and sorrowful without breaking into grief.

Duke Ai asked Tsai Wo about the altars to the spirits of the land. Tsai Wo said: The Hsia kings planted pine around them, the men of Yin planted cypress, and the men of Chau planted chestnut — chestnut, they said, to make the people tremble. When the Master heard it, he said: What is done, do not preach about; what has run its course, do not push against; what is past, do not blame.

The Master said: How small a vessel was Kwan Chung! Someone said: Was Kwan Chung frugal, then? The Master said: Kwan kept three separate establishments, and none of his officers held a second post — how can you call him frugal? Then did Kwan Chung at least know ritual? The Master said: The ruler of a state screens his gate; Kwan too screened his gate. When two rulers meet in friendship, they have a stand for the inverted cups; Kwan too had such a stand. If Kwan Chung knew ritual, then who does not?

The Master said to the grand music-master of Lu: Music can be understood. It begins with all the parts sounding as one; as it unfolds they move in harmony, each clear and distinct, flowing on unbroken — and so to the close.

The border warden at Yi asked to be presented to the Master, saying: When men of worth have passed this way, I have never been refused the meeting. The followers brought him in, and when he came out he said: My friends, why be troubled that your master has lost his post? The world has long been without the way; Heaven is about to make of your master a bell to rouse it.
The Master said of the Shao music that it was perfectly beautiful and perfectly good. Of the Wu music he said it was perfectly beautiful but not perfectly good.
The Master said: High place held without generosity; ritual performed without reverence; mourning gone through without grief — how could I bear to look on such things?
books.title: On Ritual and Music

books.label: Book IV
paragraphs: The Master said: It is the humaneness of a neighborhood that makes it good. If a man, in choosing where to settle, does not settle among the humane, how can he be called wise?
The Master said: Those without humaneness cannot rest for long in hardship, nor for long in ease. The humane are at home in their humaneness; the wise turn it to good use.
The Master said: Only the humane man knows how to love others, and how to hate them.
The Master said: Once the will is set on humaneness, there is no room left for doing wrong.

The Master said: Wealth and rank are what men desire; but if they cannot be had in the right way, do not hold on to them. Poverty and obscurity are what men dislike; but if they cannot be escaped in the right way, do not escape them. If a cultivated person abandons humaneness, how can he live up to the name? The cultivated person does not part from humaneness for the space of a single meal. In moments of haste he holds fast to it; in times of danger he holds fast to it.

The Master said: I have never seen a man who truly loved humaneness, nor one who truly hated what is inhumane. A man who loved humaneness would prize nothing above it. A man who hated what is inhumane would so practice humaneness that nothing inhumane could come near him. Is anyone able, for a single day, to put all his strength into humaneness? I have never seen a man whose strength was not enough. There may be such a case — but I have never seen it.
The Master said: A man's faults belong to his kind. Look closely at a man's faults, and you will know whether he is humane.
The Master said: If in the morning a man hears the Way, in the evening he may die content.
The Master said: A man of learning whose heart is set on the Way, yet who is ashamed of poor clothes and poor food, is not worth talking to.
The Master said: In his dealings with the world, the cultivated person is neither for anything nor against anything; he sides with what is right.
The Master said: The cultivated person thinks of virtue; the small man thinks of comfort. The cultivated person thinks of the law; the small man thinks of favors.
The Master said: A man who acts always with an eye to his own gain will stir up much resentment.
The Master said: If a ruler can govern with the courtesy that ritual asks for, what difficulty will he have? If he cannot govern with that courtesy, what has he to do with ritual at all?
The Master said: Do not be troubled that you have no position; be troubled that you are not fit for one. Do not be troubled that no one knows you; seek to be worth knowing.

The Master said: Shan, my Way is threaded on a single thread. Master Tsang said: Yes. When the Master had gone out, the other disciples asked: What did he mean? Master Tsang said: The Way of the Master is just this — wholeheartedness toward others, and weighing their hearts as your own. That, and nothing more.
The Master said: The cultivated person understands what is right; the small man understands what is profitable.
The Master said: When you see a worthy person, think of equaling him; when you see an unworthy one, turn inward and examine yourself.

The Master said: In serving his parents, a son may remonstrate with them, but gently. If he sees they are not inclined to follow him, he is all the more respectful and does not cross them, and though it wears him out, he does not complain.
The Master said: While his parents are alive, a son should not travel far; and if he does go, he must have a fixed destination.
The Master said: If for three years a son does not depart from his father's ways, he may be called a devoted son.
The Master said: A son must always keep his parents' age in mind — on the one hand for joy, on the other for fear.
The Master said: The reason the ancients were slow to speak was that they were ashamed to let their deeds fall short of their words.
The Master said: Those who hold themselves in check rarely go wrong.
The Master said: The cultivated person wishes to be slow in speech and quick in action.
The Master said: Virtue is never left to stand alone. A man who has it will have neighbors.
Tsze-yu said: Pester a ruler too often, and you bring disgrace on yourself. Reprove a friend too often, and you drive him away.
books.title: On Humaneness

books.label: Book V
paragraphs: The Master said of Kung-ye Ch'ang that he was fit to marry: though he had once been put in chains, it was through no crime of his own. And he gave him his own daughter in marriage. Of Nan Yung he said that in a well-governed state he would not be passed over for office, and in a badly governed one he would keep clear of punishment and disgrace. And he gave him his elder brother's daughter in marriage.
The Master said of Tsze-chien: A man of fine character, this one! Yet if Lu had no men of worth, where would he have gotten it?
Tsze-kung asked: And what do you make of me? The Master said: You are a vessel. What vessel? A jeweled vessel for the sacrifice.

Someone said: Yung is humane, but he has no gift for talk. The Master said: What is the good of a gift for talk? Meet people with a quick tongue and you mostly earn their dislike. Whether he is humane I do not know — but what does he want with a quick tongue?
The Master was urging Ch'i-tiao K'ai to take office. He answered: I cannot yet feel sure of myself in this. The Master was pleased.

The Master said: My way makes no headway. I will get on a raft and put out to sea. The one who would come with me — that would be Yu, I think. Tsze-lu, hearing this, was delighted. The Master said: Yu loves daring more than I do, but he has nowhere to find his timber.

Mang Wu asked whether Tsze-lu was humane. The Master said: I do not know. He asked again. The Master said: In a state of a thousand chariots, Yu could be put in charge of the military levies — but whether he is humane I do not know. And Ch'iu? The Master said: In a town of a thousand households, or a clan of a hundred chariots, Ch'iu could be made its governor — but whether he is humane I do not know. And Ch'ih? The Master said: Standing in his sash at court, Ch'ih could be set to deal with the guests and envoys — but whether he is humane I do not know.

The Master said to Tsze-kung: Which is the better, you or Hui? He answered: How could I dare compare myself with Hui? Hui hears one thing and understands ten; I hear one thing and understand two. The Master said: You are not his equal. I grant you — you and I are both not his equal.

Tsai Yu was asleep in the daytime. The Master said: Rotten wood cannot be carved, a wall of dung cannot be plastered. With Yu — what is the use of reproaching him? The Master said: There was a time when I heard a man's words and trusted his conduct; now I hear his words and watch his conduct. It is Yu who has made me change.
The Master said: I have never seen a man truly unbending. Someone said: There is Shan Ch'ang. The Master said: Ch'ang is ruled by his cravings — how can he be unbending?
Tsze-kung said: What I do not want others to do to me, I also want not to do to others. The Master said: Ts'ze, that is beyond you yet.
Tsze-kung said: One can hear the Master on questions of culture and conduct. One cannot hear him on the nature of man or the way of Heaven.
When Tsze-lu had heard something and had not yet been able to act on it, his one fear was that he might hear something more.
Tsze-kung asked: Why was Kung-wan given the title "Cultured"? The Master said: He was quick and a lover of learning, and not ashamed to ask of those beneath him. That is why he was called "Cultured."

The Master said of Tsze-ch'an that he had four marks of the cultivated man: in his own bearing he was humble; in serving those above him, respectful; in providing for the people, kind; in directing the people, just.
The Master said: Yen P'ing knew how to keep a friendship. However long he had known a man, he showed him the same respect as at first.
The Master said: Tsang Wan housed his great tortoise in a hall with mountains carved on the pillar-tops and waterweed painted on the beams. What sort of wisdom was that?

Tsze-chang asked: The minister Tsze-wan took office three times and showed no joy, and three times was dismissed and showed no resentment; each time he handed the old government over fully to his successor. What do you make of him? The Master said: He was loyal. Was he humane? The Master said: I do not know — how does that make him humane? Tsze-chang went on: When Ts'ui killed the prince of Ch'i, Ch'an Wan, who owned forty horses, abandoned them and left the country. Coming to another state, he said, "They are no better here than our own officer Ts'ui," and left. He came to a second state, said the same, and left again. What do you make of him? The Master said: He was clean. Was he humane? The Master said: I do not know — how does that make him humane?
Chi Wan thought three times before he acted. The Master, hearing of it, said: Twice is enough.
The Master said: When the country was well governed, Ning Wu played the wise man; when it fell into disorder, he played the fool. His wisdom others may match — his folly they cannot.

When the Master was in Ch'an he said: Let me go home! Let me go home! The young ones of my school are headstrong and rash; they have made a fine, finished start, but do not know how to cut and shape themselves.
The Master said: Po-i and Shu-ch'i held no man's old wrongs against him, and so they were little resented.
The Master said: Who calls Wei-shang Kao straight? A man begged vinegar of him, and he begged it from a neighbor and gave it as his own.

The Master said: Smooth words, a fawning look, and overdone respect — Tso Ch'iu-ming was ashamed of them, and so am I. To hide a grudge against a man and act the friend to him — Tso Ch'iu-ming was ashamed of that, and so am I.

Yen Yuan and Chi Lu were at his side. The Master said: Why not each of you tell me what you long for? Tsze-lu said: I would have my carriage and horses and fine fur coats to share with my friends, and not mind if they wore them out. Yen Yuan said: I would not boast of my goodness or make a show of my labors. Tsze-lu said: And now we would hear the Master's longing. The Master said: To give the old their rest, to give friends my trust, and to cherish the young.
The Master said: It is hopeless! I have yet to meet the man who can see his own faults and arraign himself within.
The Master said: In a hamlet of ten households there is sure to be someone as loyal and true as I am — but none so fond of learning.
books.title: Judgments of Disciples

books.label: Book VI
paragraphs: The Master said: There is Yung — he could be seated facing south, like a prince. Chung-kung asked about Tsze-sang Po-tsze. The Master said: He will do; he does not fuss over small matters. Chung-kung said: To hold reverence within yourself and yet keep an easy hand in small matters when you govern the people — that may pass. But to be easy within and easy without as well — is that not too easy by far? The Master said: Yung is right.

Duke Ai asked which of the disciples loved learning. Confucius answered: There was Yen Hui; he loved to learn. He never turned his anger on the wrong person, and he never made the same mistake twice. Sadly, his life was cut short and he died; and now there is no one like him. I have not heard of anyone since who loves learning as he did.

When Tsze-hwa was sent on a mission to Ch'i, the disciple Zan asked for grain to provide for Tsze-hwa's mother. The Master said: Give her a fu. Zan asked for more. Give her an yu, said the Master. Zan gave her five ping. The Master said: When Ch'ih set out for Ch'i, he had sleek horses to his carriage and wore fine furs. I have heard that the cultivated person relieves the hard-pressed, but does not add to the riches of the rich.

When Yuan Sze was made governor of his town, the Master granted him nine hundred measures of grain, and Sze declined them. The Master said: Do not refuse. Could you not pass them on to the neighborhoods, the hamlets, and the villages around you?

Speaking of Chung-kung, the Master said: If the calf of a plowing ox is red-coated and well-horned, then even if men would rather not offer it, will the spirits of the mountains and rivers turn it away?
The Master said: Such was Hui — for three months together his heart would not stray from humaneness. The others may reach it for a day or a month, and no more.

Chi K'ang asked whether Chung-yu was fit to hold office. The Master said: Yu is decisive; what trouble would he have holding office? And is Ts'ze fit to hold office? The Master said: Ts'ze sees into things; what trouble would he have holding office? And Ch'iu? The Master said: Ch'iu has many talents; what trouble would he have holding office?

The head of the Chi family sent to make Min Tsze-ch'ien governor of Pi. Min Tsze-ch'ien said: Make my excuses for me, gently. If anyone comes asking a second time, I shall have to cross the Wan and leave the country.

When Po-niu was ill, the Master went to ask after him. He took his hand through the window and said: He is lost — it is the will of Heaven, alas. That such a man should have such a sickness! That such a man should have such a sickness!

The Master said: What a fine character Hui had! A bowl of rice, a gourd of water, a poor man's lane to live in — others could not have borne such misery, yet it never spoiled Hui's joy. What a fine character Hui had!

Yen Ch'iu said: It is not that I take no delight in your Way; my strength is not enough for it. The Master said: Those whose strength is not enough give out halfway along the road. You are drawing your own line before you start.
The Master said to Tsze-hsia: Be a scholar in the manner of the cultivated person, not in the manner of the small man.

When Tsze-yu was governor of Wu-ch'ang, the Master asked: Have you found any good men there? He answered: There is Tan-t'ai Mieh-ming. He never takes a shortcut when he walks, and he never comes to my office except on public business.

The Master said: Mang Chih-fan never boasts of what he does. When the army was in flight he brought up the rear, and as they reached the gate he whipped his horse forward and said: It was not that I dared to come last — my horse would not go any faster.
The Master said: Without the smooth tongue of the priest T'o and the good looks of Prince Chao of Sung, it is hard to get through these times unscathed.
The Master said: Who can go out except by the door? Why, then, will no one walk by this Way?

The Master said: Where the raw stuff outweighs the polish, a man is coarse; where the polish outweighs the raw stuff, he is a mere clerk. Raw stuff and polish in even measure — there you have the cultivated person.
The Master said: A man is born for uprightness. If a man loses it and lives on, he has only luck to thank that he is not dead.
The Master said: Those who know it are not equal to those who love it; and those who love it are not equal to those who delight in it.
The Master said: To those above the common run you may speak of the highest things; to those below it you may not.

Fan Ch'ih asked what wisdom is. The Master said: To give yourself wholly to the duties owed to other people, and to honor the spirits while keeping your distance from them — that may be called wisdom. He asked about humaneness. The Master said: The humane person takes on the hard part first and lets the reward come after — that may be called humaneness.
The Master said: The wise delight in water; the humane delight in mountains. The wise are active; the humane are still. The wise find joy; the humane find length of days.
The Master said: Ch'i, with one change, would rise to the level of Lu; and Lu, with one change, would rise to the level of the Way.
The Master said: A drinking-cup that is no longer a cup — what a cup! What a cup!

Tsai Wo asked: Suppose a humane man were told there was someone down a well — would he go in after him? The Master said: Why would he do that? You may send the cultivated person to the well, but you cannot make him jump in; you may deceive him, but you cannot make a fool of him.
The Master said: The cultivated person studies widely in all learning, and reins himself in with ritual; so he too can keep from overstepping what is right.
When the Master had been to see Nan-tsze, Tsze-lu was displeased. The Master swore an oath: If I have done anything wrong, may Heaven cast me off! May Heaven cast me off!
The Master said: The virtue of the Constant Mean — how perfect it is! And how long it has been rare among the people.

Tsze-kung said: Suppose a man who showered benefits on the people and could bring help to all — what would you say of him? Could he be called humane? The Master said: Why stop at humane? Surely he would be a sage. Even Yao and Shun fell short of that. As for the humane person: wishing to stand on his own feet, he helps others to stand; wishing to reach his goal, he helps others to reach theirs. To take what is near at hand — yourself — as the measure of others: that may be called the practice of humaneness.
books.title: On Disciples and the Humane Life

books.label: Book VII
paragraphs: The Master said: A transmitter and not a maker, trusting and loving the ancients — in this I venture to liken myself to our old P'ang.
The Master said: To store up knowledge in silence, to learn without ever tiring, to teach others without growing weary — which of these have I mastered?

The Master said: That I leave my character untended, that I fail to dig deep into what I learn, that I hear what is right and cannot move toward it, that I see my faults and cannot mend them — these are the things that trouble me.
When the Master was at his ease, his manner was relaxed and his face content.
The Master said: How far I have declined! It is a long time now since I dreamed, as I used to, of the duke of Chau.
The Master said: Set your heart on the Way. Hold fast to virtue. Lean on humaneness. And find your recreation in the arts.
The Master said: From the man who brought no more than a bundle of dried meat for my teaching, I have never withheld instruction.

The Master said: I do not open the way for one who is not burning to understand, nor help out one who is not struggling to put his thought into words. When I have shown a man one corner and he cannot come back to me with the other three, I do not go on.
When the Master ate beside someone in mourning, he never ate his fill. On a day he had wept, he did not sing.

The Master said to Yen Yuan: To take up office when you are called, and to retire quietly when you are not — only you and I can do this. Tsze-lu said: If you had charge of the armies of a great state, whom would you take with you? The Master said: Not the man who would fight a tiger bare-handed or wade a river with no boat, and die without a second thought. The one I want is the one who comes to the work wary, who loves to lay his plans, and so brings them off.
The Master said: If riches could be had for the seeking, I would seek them, even with whip in hand as a groom. But since they cannot, I will follow what I love.
The things the Master treated with the most care were fasting, war, and sickness.
When the Master was in Ch'i, he heard the Shao music, and for three months did not notice the taste of meat. He said: I never imagined that music could reach such heights.

Yen Yu said: Is the Master for the ruler of Wei? Tsze-kung said: I will go and ask him. He went in and said: What sort of men were Po-i and Shu-ch'i? The Master said: They were worthy men of old. And did they nurse any regret? The Master said: They sought humaneness, and they found it — what was there to regret? Tsze-kung came out and said: The Master is not for him.
The Master said: With coarse rice to eat, water to drink, and my bent arm for a pillow — even so I have joy. Riches and honor gotten by wrong are to me a passing cloud.
The Master said: Give me a few more years — fifty for the study of the Yi — and I might come through without grave faults.
The Master often spoke of the Odes, the History, and the keeping of ritual. On these he spoke often.

The Duke of Sheh asked Tsze-lu about Confucius, and Tsze-lu gave him no answer. The Master said: Why did you not simply tell him — here is a man who in his hunger for knowledge forgets to eat, who in his joy forgets his cares, and does not notice old age coming on?
The Master said: I am not one who was born knowing. I love the ancients, and I work hard to seek it there.
The Master did not talk of marvels, of feats of strength, of disorder, or of spirits.
The Master said: Walking with two others, I am sure of a teacher in them. I pick out what is good in them and follow it; what is bad, and mend it in myself.
The Master said: Heaven planted the virtue that is in me. Hwan T'ui — what can he do to me?
The Master said: Do you think, my friends, that I keep anything back? I keep nothing back from you. There is nothing I do that I do not share with you — that is my way.
The Master taught four things: letters, conduct, faithfulness, and good faith.

The Master said: A sage I cannot hope to see; if I could see a person of real worth, that would be enough. The Master said: A good man I cannot hope to see; if I could see a man of constancy, that would be enough. To have nothing and act as if you had, to be empty and act as if you were full, to be in want and act as if you were at ease — it is hard for such a man to have constancy.
The Master fished, but not with a net. He shot, but not at roosting birds.

The Master said: There may be those who act without knowing why; I am not one of them. To hear much, pick out the good, and follow it; to see much and hold it in mind — this is the next best thing to knowing.

The people of Hu-hsiang were hard to talk with, and when a boy from there was received by the Master, the disciples were uneasy. The Master said: I take a man as he comes to me; I do not answer for what he does once he leaves. Why be so harsh? When a man cleanses himself to come to me, I welcome the man he now is; I do not vouch for his past.
The Master said: Is humaneness so far off? I want to be humane, and there — humaneness is here.

The minister of crime of Ch'an asked whether Duke Chao knew ritual. Confucius said: He knew ritual. When Confucius had gone, the minister beckoned Wu-ma Ch'i forward and said: I had heard that the cultivated person takes no sides. Can he too take sides? The prince married a woman of the house of Wu, of his own surname, and called her "the elder Tsze of Wu." If this prince knew ritual, who does not? Wu-ma Ch'i reported this. The Master said: I am a lucky man. If I make a mistake, others are sure to know it.
When the Master was with someone who was singing and sang well, he would have him sing it again, and then join in.
The Master said: In letters I am perhaps no worse than other men. But to live out in my own conduct what the cultivated person professes — that I have not yet reached.

The Master said: A sage, or a man of perfect humaneness — how could I dare claim to be either? But that I strive toward it without tiring, and teach others without weariness — that much may be said of me. Kung-hsi Hwa said: And that is just what we, your disciples, cannot learn to do.

The Master was gravely ill, and Tsze-lu asked leave to pray for him. The Master said: Is there such a thing? Tsze-lu said: There is. The Eulogies say, "Prayer has been made for you to the spirits above and below." The Master said: Then my praying has been going on a long while.
The Master said: Extravagance breeds insolence, and stinginess breeds meanness. Better mean than insolent.
The Master said: The cultivated person is calm and at ease; the small man is always anxious and on edge.
The Master was gentle, yet firm; commanding, yet not harsh; respectful, yet at ease.
books.title: The Master's Own Way

books.label: Book VIII
paragraphs: The Master said: T'ai-po may be said to have reached the very height of virtue. Three times he gave up the empire, and so quietly that the people never even knew enough to praise him.

The Master said: Respectfulness without ritual becomes wearisome fuss; caution without ritual becomes timidity; boldness without ritual becomes rebellion; plain speaking without ritual becomes rudeness. When those in high place are devoted to their own kin, the people are stirred to humaneness; when they do not forget their old friends, the people are kept from meanness.

Master Tsang was gravely ill, and called his disciples to him and said: Uncover my feet, uncover my hands. The Book of Poetry says, "In fear and trembling, as on the brink of a deep gulf, as treading thin ice." But now, my little children, I know that I have come through, my body whole.

Master Tsang was ill, and Meng Chang came to ask after him. Master Tsang said to him: When a bird is about to die, its cry is mournful; when a man is about to die, his words are good. There are three things the man of high rank should hold most important: that in his bearing and manner he keep clear of violence and carelessness; that in his looks he stay close to sincerity; and that in his words and tone he keep far from coarseness and impropriety. As for the sacrificial vessels, there are officers to see to those.

Master Tsang said: Gifted, yet asking of those who were not; full of knowledge, yet asking of those who had little; having, yet as though he had not; full, yet counting himself empty; wronged, yet picking no quarrel — I once had a friend who lived like this.

Master Tsang said: Suppose a man you could trust with a young orphaned prince, and charge with the rule of a domain of a hundred li, and whom no crisis, however great, could shake from his principles — is such a man a cultivated person? A cultivated person indeed.

Master Tsang said: The scholar cannot be without breadth of mind and tough endurance, for his burden is heavy and his road is long. Humaneness is the burden he takes as his own — is it not heavy? Only with death does the road end — is it not long?
The Master said: Roused by the Odes; established by ritual; perfected by music.
The Master said: The people may be made to follow a path, but not to understand it.
The Master said: A man who loves daring and chafes at poverty will turn to rebellion; and a man who is without humaneness, if you push your dislike of him too far, will turn to it as well.
The Master said: Though a man had gifts as splendid as the Duke of Chau's, if he were proud and stingy the rest would not be worth a glance.
The Master said: It is not easy to find a man who can study three years without his mind turning to a salary.

The Master said: Hold fast to sincerity, love learning, and guard the good way to the death. Do not enter a tottering state, nor stay in one in disorder. When the way prevails in the world, show yourself; when it does not, keep hidden. When a country is well governed, poverty and obscurity are a disgrace; when a country is badly governed, wealth and rank are a disgrace.
The Master said: If you do not hold the office, do not meddle in its business.
The Master said: When the music-master Chih began, and the close of the Kwan Tsu came — how it filled the ears!
The Master said: Ardent but not upright; ignorant but not careful; simple but not honest — such people are beyond me.
The Master said: Study as though you could never catch up, and as though you feared to lose what you had.
The Master said: How lofty was the way Shun and Yü held the empire — as if it were nothing to them!

The Master said: Great indeed was Yao as a ruler! How lofty! Heaven alone is grand, and Yao alone matched it. So vast was his virtue that the people could find no name for it. How lofty in all he accomplished, how brilliant in the forms and laws he set up!

Shun had five ministers, and the empire was well governed. King Wu said, "I have ten able ministers." Confucius said: How true the saying, that talent is hard to find! Only at the meeting of the houses of T'ang and Yü was it more abundant than in this age of Chau — and even then there was a woman among them, so the able men were no more than nine. King Wan held two parts of the empire in three, and with them still served the house of Yin. The virtue of the house of Chau may be called the very height of virtue.

The Master said: In Yü I can find no flaw. His own food and drink were poor, yet he was lavish in devotion to the spirits. His everyday clothes were plain, yet his sacrificial cap and apron were of the finest. He lived in a mean low house, yet poured out all his strength on the ditches and channels. In Yü I can find no flaw.
books.title: T'ai-po, and the Burden of the Scholar

books.label: Book IX
paragraphs: The Master rarely spoke of profit, or of fate, or of humaneness.

A man of the village of Ta-hsiang said: How great is K'ung! His learning is vast, yet there is no one thing that has made his name. The Master heard of it and said to his disciples: What, then, should I take up? Should I take up charioteering, or archery? Let me take up charioteering.

The Master said: The linen cap is what ritual prescribes; but nowadays men wear silk, which is cheaper, and in this I follow the common practice. Ritual prescribes bowing below the hall; but nowadays men bow only after they have gone up, which is arrogant. Here I keep to the old way and bow below the hall, even against the common practice.
There were four things the Master had wholly put away: he formed no foregone conclusions, laid down no rigid rules, was never obstinate, and was never self-centered.

When the Master was held in fear at K'wang, he said: King Wan is dead, but is not the cause of culture lodged here in me? Had Heaven meant this culture to perish, it would not have placed it in the hands of one born after him. And since Heaven does not mean it to perish, what can the men of K'wang do to me?

A high officer asked Tsze-kung: Surely your Master is a sage? How many things he can do! Tsze-kung said: Heaven has indeed set him on the way to sagehood, and given him many gifts besides. When the Master heard of it he said: Does the high officer know me? When I was young I was of low station, and so I learned many humble skills. But must the cultivated person be a man of many skills? No, he need not be. And Lao said: The Master used to say, "It was because I held no office that I picked up so many arts."
The Master said: Do I have knowledge? I have none. But when some plain man with an empty mind puts a question to me, I tap it at both ends, and search it out to the last.
The Master said: The phoenix does not come; the river gives up no chart. It is all over with me.

When the Master saw anyone in mourning dress, or in the cap and robes of full ceremony, or anyone who was blind, then even if they were younger than he, he would rise; and if he had to pass them, he passed quickly.

Yen Yuan, sighing, said: The more I look up to it, the higher it goes; the harder I bore into it, the firmer it grows. I see it ahead of me, and of a sudden it is behind. Step by step the Master leads us on with skill. He broadened me with culture and reined me in with ritual. When I would give it up, I cannot; and after I have spent all my strength, there it stands, sheer above me — yet for all my wish to follow, I find no way to reach it.

The Master was gravely ill, and Tsze-lu had the disciples act as if they were the household officers of a great man. In a lull in the illness the Master said: Long has Yu kept up this pretense! To make believe I have officers when I have none — whom would I be deceiving? Would I deceive Heaven? And better that I die in the hands of you, my disciples, than in the hands of officers. Even if I get no grand funeral, am I going to die by the roadside?
Tsze-kung said: Here is a fine gem. Shall I shut it in a case and keep it, or look for a good price and sell it? The Master said: Sell it! Sell it! But I would wait for the right price.

The Master wished to go and live among the nine wild tribes of the east. Someone said: They are rude. How could you? The Master said: If a cultivated person lived among them, what rudeness would be left?
The Master said: It was after I came back from Wei to Lu that the music was set right, and the Court hymns and the hymns of praise each found their proper place.

The Master said: To serve the high ministers and nobles abroad, and at home to serve my father and elder brothers; to do all that is owed to the dead, sparing no effort; and never to be mastered by wine — which of these have I managed?
Standing by a river, the Master said: It flows on like this, never stopping, day or night.
The Master said: I have never seen a man who loved virtue as he loves a beautiful face.

The Master said: It is like raising a mound. If I stop one basket short of finishing, I have stopped, and the stopping is mine. It is like leveling ground. Though I have thrown down but one basket, if I go forward, the going forward is mine.
The Master said: The one who never flagged when I set something before him — that was Hui.
The Master said of Yen Yuan: Alas! I watched him always going forward; I never once saw him stop.
The Master said: There are shoots that never come to flower, and there are flowers that never come to fruit.

The Master said: The young are to be held in awe. How do we know that those coming after will not match the men of today? But if a man reaches forty or fifty and has made no name, then there is nothing in him to hold in awe.

The Master said: Words of stern reproof — can a man help but assent to them? But it is the mending of his ways that matters. Words of gentle counsel — can a man help but be pleased with them? But it is the working out of their drift that matters. With a man who is pleased and never works it out, who assents and never mends his ways, I can do nothing at all.
The Master said: Hold faithfulness and sincerity above all. Take no friend who is not your equal in this. And when you are wrong, do not be afraid to set it right.
The Master said: You may carry off the commander of a great army, but you cannot carry off the will of even a common man.

The Master said: Standing in a tattered hemp-quilted coat beside men dressed in furs, and not ashamed — that is Yu. "He grudges nothing, he covets nothing; how can he do anything but good?" Tsze-lu took to reciting these lines over and over, until the Master said: This much is hardly enough to make a man good.
The Master said: Only when the year turns cold do we see that the pine and the cypress are the last to lose their leaves.
The Master said: The wise are free of doubt, the humane free of anxiety, the bold free of fear.

The Master said: There are men you can study beside who cannot go with you toward the Way; men who can go toward the Way with you, yet cannot stand firm in it beside you; men who can stand firm beside you, yet cannot weigh the changing case beside you.
